name: Kids in Need of Defense: legal services and regional work (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: by share of the result at the defaults: the US casework (91%; the children live in the US), the CAM refugee applicants in Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador (8%, by KIND's clients' countries of origin) and psychosocial support in Mexico and for Ukrainian children (1%).
summary: Kids in Need of Defense (KIND) represents unaccompanied migrant children in US immigration proceedings through its own lawyers and about 4,600 pro bono attorneys, and supports children in Mexico, Central America and Europe; in 2024 it served 8,500 children in the US and closed 580 cases with permanent relief (asylum, green cards, T and U visas). This model values a child's permanent status by a life in the US instead of removal to Guatemala, Honduras or El Salvador (for the 30% judged to be removed without it) or a life with status instead of undocumented, plus the danger at home avoided; with about half that relief judged not to have come without KIND and three quarters of the credit KIND's (the rest the pro bono lawyers' time at their own wage), it comes to about 0.013 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, because KIND's own spending comes to roughly $100,000 for each permanent relief and most children left without status are never removed. The biggest uncertainties are the chance of removal without status and what a lawyer changes, both judged from observational data, so all four branches (US casework, Central American Minors refugee applications, psychosocial support in Mexico and for Ukrainian children, and the other children served outside the US) are discounted by the shared missing-data slider; KIND's advocacy is a separate model.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

rows.label: Cost of the two programmes with their share of overhead
Average real spending over the years the closed cases ran, over 2024's
rows.explainer: The cases that closed with permanent relief in 2024 were worked on over the years before (asylum and Special Immigrant Juvenile cases take years, and green cards for SIJS youth from Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador waited years for a visa number), while KIND's spending grew fast, so the year's relief is set against the average real spending of those years, not 2024's alone (Convention 11's same-period rule). KIND, Inc.'s Form 990 total functional expenses (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, EIN 26-2763038): $23.1 million in 2019, $31.3 million in 2020, $41.7 million in 2021, $53.5 million in 2022, $67.4 million in 2023 and $79.6 million in 2024. In 2024 prices (@cpi.usa) the 2021-2024 average is 0.80 of 2024's, 2022-2024 0.86 and 2019-2024 0.67. Our judgment 0.8 (cases about four years long), from 0.67 (six) to 0.86 (three).

source.page: p. 5; p. 9, Impact by the Numbers ('580 Cases Closed with Permanent Legal Relief')
source.quote: In the United States, approximately 580 clients' legal cases closed, having received permanent legal relief in the form of asylum, adjustment of status to lawful permanent residence, T-visa approval, or U-visa approval.

rows.explainer: KIND's own count. A child's case runs for years and ends in relief only once; the relief closed in a year is the yearly flow (Convention 3). Special Immigrant Juvenile approvals, deferred action and dismissals on the way are not added: they lead to the green cards counted here.

rows.label: Children gaining permanent relief a year, at 2024's scale of work, per child served
rows.explainer: The year's relief cases scaled to 2024's spending (above), over the children served: about 8.5%. KIND says it wins over 95% of the cases it carries to their end (2023 report), but most cases are still open, move with the child or end otherwise.

rows.label: Death rate of a young person returned to northern Central America
rows.explainer: The shared KIND figure (facts/kind.json): 0.0025 a year in the first years back, from 0.0012 to 0.005.

rows.label: Death rate at the same ages in the US
rows.explainer: The shared KIND figure: only the excess over it counts.

rows.label: Chance a child left without status is removed
rows.explainer: The shared KIND figure: 30%, from 10% to 60%; the rest stay in the US undocumented.

rows.label: Share of the children served whose removal the year's relief averts
rows.explainer: A child who gains permanent status stays; without it, the share above would have been removed and faced the danger they fled.

rows.label: Years a returned young person faces the excess danger
rows.explainer: The shared KIND figure: 3 years, from 1 to 5.

rows.label: Deaths averted per child served
rows.explainer: Excess deaths over the years of danger, discounted at the shared rate, times the share whose removal is averted.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: None: KIND's clients are children who travelled alone, almost all over five and most of them teenagers.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one value of a death by age band (@moral_weights), ages 5-14 and 15-49 split by the shared KIND share (@kind.share_5_14), times your value of a life.

rows.label: Clients' families' consumption per person a year at home (2024 US$)
rows.explainer: The survey means of Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador (@survey_consumption, 2021 PPP dollars a day), weighted by KIND's clients' countries of origin (88% of clients; the rest taken at the same mix), times the clients' families' share of the mean (@kind.client_consumption_vs_mean, 0.6), over the year, in 2024 US prices so it compares with the US survey figure below. About $3,300.

rows.label: Consumption per person a year of a young immigrant in the US (2024 US$)
rows.explainer: US household-survey spending per person (Consumer Expenditure Survey 2024) times the share poor newcomers consume (@irap.destination_consumption_share, 0.45, the lowest fifth's: the same figure as for refugees resettled in the US). About $14,700.

rows.label: A year in the US instead of at home, on the log scale
rows.explainer: About {{row:ln_gain_removed}}: consumption about 4.5 times higher.

rows.label: A year with legal status instead of undocumented in the US, on the log scale
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/united_states.json): 0.1 on the log scale, from 0.04 to 0.25, from the 1986 amnesty's wage gains plus the work authorisation, benefits and credit status brings.

rows.label: Discounted years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: The shared KIND figure (40 years, from 25 to 55), discounted at the shared rate: about 20.6 at 4%.

rows.label: Log-consumption gain per child served
rows.explainer: For a child who gains permanent status: with the chance they would have been removed, a life in the US instead of at home; otherwise, the same life with status instead of without (about 10% more consumption); for the discounted years the gain lasts; times the share gaining relief. About 0.8 log points per child served.

rows.label: Illness averted per child served, in DALYs
rows.explainer: Not counted separately: the anxiety of a pending case and the health care status opens are in the unmodelled shares below rather than guessed as disability weights.

rows.label: US casework: units of value before adjustments
People given legal assistance with Central American Minors (CAM) refugee applications, 2024

source.title: KIND, A Year of Readiness and Resilience: Annual Report 2024 (archived copy: web.archive.org; the site sits behind a bot check)
source.page: p. 6, Reuniting Families: Central American Minors Program, Key Achievements

rows.explainer: Children in Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador applying through the CAM programme to join a parent lawfully in the US, and their families, helped by KIND's staff and pro bono network; in December 2024 KIND represented three children at CAM interviews, all granted refugee status. Part of the regional work.

rows.label: Share of the CAM applicants assisted who reach the US
rows.explainer: KIND publishes no count of arrivals. CAM applicants who reach interview are mostly approved, but processing takes a year or more and the programme stopped with the US refugee suspension of 20 January 2025, leaving most 2024 applicants who had not yet travelled stranded. Our judgment 15%, from 5% to 40%; whether they would have arrived without KIND is the counterfactual below.

rows.label: Value of a child's move to the US (units of value)
rows.formula: ln_gain_removed * gain_years_pv * $uov_per_ln_consumption + (crisis_mortality_rate - baseline_mortality_rate) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, years_exposed) * value_per_death
rows.explainer: The same value as a removal averted in the US branch: a life at US instead of home consumption for the discounted years the gain lasts, plus the excess danger at home avoided.

source.title: KIND, A Year of Readiness and Resilience: Annual Report 2024 (archived copy: web.archive.org; the site sits behind a bot check)

rows.label: Children given psychosocial support outside the US
Effect of focused psychosocial support for children in humanitarian settings (SD)

source.title: Purgato M. et al., Focused psychosocial interventions for children in low-resource humanitarian settings: a systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis, Lancet Global Health 2018; 6(4): e390-e400
source.quote: Benefits were also found at endpoint for functional impairment (-0·29, -0·43 to -0·15)

rows.explainer: 11 randomised trials, 3,143 children, against waiting lists: PTSD symptoms fell by 0.33 SD and functional impairment by 0.29 SD at the end of treatment, smaller at follow-up (0.21 for PTSD), with weaker effects for displaced children. We take functioning's 0.29, its 95% interval as the range, as the wellbeing effect; how far KIND's case management and groups resemble the trialled programmes is in the evidence adjustment.

rows.label: How long the effect lasts, fading linearly (years)
rows.explainer: The trials' effects were still about two thirds of the endpoint at follow-ups of a few months; children in transit move on quickly. One year to fade out, from half a year to two.

rows.label: WELLBYs per child supported
rows.explainer: The effect in SDs, fading linearly over its duration (× 0.5), in WELLBYs by the shared factor (@wellby_factors.wellbys_per_sd_year, 2 points of life satisfaction per SD-year).

rows.label: Psychosocial support: WELLBYs before adjustments
Children KIND served worldwide, 2024

source.title: KIND, A Year of Readiness and Resilience: Annual Report 2024 (archived copy: web.archive.org; the site sits behind a bot check)
source.page: p. 5; p. 9, Impact by the Numbers ('13,000+ Children Served Globally')
source.quote: KIND staff and pro bono attorneys provided legal representation and assistance to more than 13,000 children globally, including 8,500 children across 16 offices within the United States.

rows.explainer: KIND's own count; the US's 8,500 are in the first branch.

rows.label: Other children served outside the US
rows.explainer: The rest of the 13,000 (about 1,800): children returned to Guatemala and Honduras in the reintegration programme (some 2,500 since 2010, a few hundred a year, with family support, schooling and vocational training), children given legal help in Mexico (asylum with COMAR, best-interest work in 108 cases) and in Europe and the UK. KIND gives no split, and some may overlap the counts above; counting them all is the generous reading, so the overlap is in the evidence adjustment below.

rows.label: Other children: WELLBYs before adjustments
rows.explainer: Valued through the same psychosocial chain (the trials' effect on functioning, fading over a year): reintegration support and legal help in transit work mostly through safety, stability and wellbeing; the reintegration programme's vocational training is in the range of the evidence adjustment rather than modelled as income.

rows.label: US casework: trust in the value of status
rows.explainer: The value of status rests on survey consumption in the home countries and the US, the place-premium literature (the same people earn several times more in the US) and legalisation studies, and the chance of removal is a judgment. 0.8, from 0.6 to 1.

rows.label: Share of KIND's relief clients who would have found other counsel
rows.explainer: The federal programme funded legal services providers in many cities (KIND was one of more than 100 subcontractors), but representation never kept up: about a third of children's pending cases had a lawyer in 2014 (TRAC), and providers turned children away for lack of capacity through 2024. Some of KIND's clients would have found another free lawyer or paid one. Our judgment 35%, from 15% to 60%.

rows.label: Relief rate of children without a lawyer, as a share of the rate with one
rows.explainer: TRAC's study of children's cases decided in fiscal years 2012-2014: 73% of represented children were allowed to remain against 15% of those who appeared alone (0.21). Some of that gap is selection (lawyers take stronger cases; children without one miss hearings), but a child without a lawyer rarely gets Special Immigrant Juvenile status, which needs a state-court order and a USCIS petition. Our judgment 0.25, from 0.12 to 0.45. Source: https://tracreports.org/immigration/reports/371/ (retrieved 2026-11-14).

rows.label: US casework: share of the relief that would not have come without KIND
rows.explainer: Relief for clients who would have had no lawyer, less the relief they would have won alone. About 0.49.

rows.label: Law-firm billing rate behind KIND's donated services (US$ an hour)
rows.explainer: KIND values donated work at the firms' rates. Anchor: in 2023 'Our partners donated $118,000,000—158,000 hours' (2023 report, p. 11), $747 an hour, matching the audited 2023 donated services ($118.8 million); a year of rate growth gives about $770 for 2024, from $700 to $850. Over its first 15 years the average was $597 (p. 3: $889 million for 1.49 million hours), at earlier years' rates.

rows.label: Pro bono hours behind the year's casework
rows.explainer: About 180,000 hours.

rows.label: Value of a pro bono hour at what the lawyers earn (US$)
rows.explainer: Convention 2 values volunteers at their own wage, not at what firms bill. Most of KIND's 4,600 pro bono attorneys work at large law firms and corporate legal departments, paid above the US lawyer median of about $73 an hour (BLS, 2024); associates' pay at large firms runs above $100. Our judgment $90, from $60 to $150.

rows.label: Pro bono time at the lawyers' own wage
rows.explainer: About $16 million, against $137 million at billing rates.

rows.label: Others' resources behind a child's relief, as a share of KIND's cost
rows.explainer: State courts' findings for Special Immigrant Juvenile petitions, USCIS's and the immigration courts' adjudication, and partner legal-aid groups' work on shared cases. These cost a few thousand dollars a case against KIND's roughly $100,000 for each relief won; our judgment 0.1, from 0.03 to 0.3.

rows.label: US casework's cost with overhead
US casework: KIND's share of the resources behind the relief
rows.explainer: KIND's cost over everyone's: its own, the volunteers' time and the others' resources above (Convention 2). About 0.75.

rows.label: Years from a year's casework to the relief it brings
rows.explainer: Relief closed in 2024 comes from work done over the years before (above): the year's work turns into status about two years later on average, from one to four.

rows.label: US casework: the wait, discounted
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: US casework: missing-data step
rows.explainer: KIND counts its relief cases, but no controlled evaluation of its representation exists: the effect of a lawyer and the chance of removal are judged from observational data, so the shared missing-data step applies (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: CAM: trust in the value of a move
rows.explainer: The same question as the US branch: the value of a life in the US instead of at home.

rows.label: CAM: share of the arrivals that would not have come without KIND
rows.explainer: CAM applications are filed through resettlement agencies and decided by US officials; KIND's legal help mostly matters for children whose cases stall (documents, parentage, interviews), and attorneys were first allowed at CAM interviews only in December 2024. Our judgment 30%, from 10% to 60%.

rows.label: CAM: KIND's share of the resources behind an arrival
rows.explainer: Resettlement agencies file the cases, the State Department and USCIS process them and pay for travel and reception: our judgment 0.5, from 0.3 to 0.8, as for the pathways IRAP's litigation opens in charityevals' model of it (0.5 with co-counsel).

rows.label: CAM: years from the year's help to arrival
rows.explainer: Interviews, security and medical checks and travel follow the application by months to years: about a year, from 0.3 to 2.

rows.label: CAM: the wait, discounted
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: CAM: missing-data step
rows.explainer: KIND counts the people assisted but not the arrivals, which are our judgment: the shared missing-data step applies.

rows.label: Psychosocial support: how far the trials apply
rows.explainer: The trials tested structured group programmes over several sessions; KIND's support in Mexico is case management, individual sessions and therapeutic groups for children in shelters and in transit, often seen briefly, and the effects were weaker for displaced children. 0.5, from 0.3 to 0.8, below the 0.8 of the casework, whose effect is better grounded.

rows.label: Psychosocial support: share that would not have been given anyway
rows.explainer: The trials' effects are already against a waiting list; the question is whether these children would have got similar support from UNICEF-supported shelters or Mexico's child-welfare system, which is thinly staffed at the border. 0.8, from 0.6 to 0.95.

rows.label: Psychosocial support: KIND's share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: KIND's staff deliver it, in shelters run by others who house and feed the children: 0.85, from 0.6 to 1.

rows.label: Psychosocial support: missing-data step
rows.explainer: KIND counts the children but measures no outcomes, and the effect comes from other programmes: the shared missing-data step applies.

rows.label: Other children: how far the psychosocial trials apply, and overlap
rows.explainer: Below the psychosocial branch's 0.5: these children get a mix of legal help, case management and reintegration support, not a trialled programme, and some of them may already be counted in the branches above. 0.3, from 0.15 to 0.6.

rows.label: Other children: share that would not have been given anyway
rows.explainer: The same question as the psychosocial branch: thinly staffed public services at the border and on return.

rows.label: Other children: KIND's share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: Partners deliver much of the reintegration programme (Pop No'j in Guatemala and others) with KIND's funding and staff; in Europe KIND works through partner NGOs and law firms. 0.7, from 0.4 to 0.9.

rows.label: Other children: missing-data step
rows.explainer: No outcome data and no split of the count: the shared missing-data step applies.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: Nothing more: the counts are relief won, people assisted and children supported, and how much each gets is in the branches' effects.

rows.label: Funging and leverage
rows.explainer: Federal contracts paid for about two thirds of KIND's own spending in 2024 (government contracts $59.0 million and grants $3.5 million); a donor's dollar paid for casework the contracts did not cover, and after the federal stop-work order of February 2025 and the end of KIND's subcontract in 2026 no government pays for it instead. 1, from 0.9 to 1.05.

rows.label: US: product of its adjustments
rows.formula: us_evidence_adj * us_counterfactual_adj * us_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * us_wait_discount * us_missing_data_adj

rows.label: CAM: product of its adjustments
rows.formula: cam_evidence_adj * cam_counterfactual_adj * cam_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * cam_wait_discount * cam_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Other children: product of its adjustments
rows.formula: oth_evidence_adj * oth_counterfactual_adj * oth_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * oth_missing_data_adj

rows.label: PSY: product of its adjustments
rows.formula: psy_evidence_adj * psy_counterfactual_adj * psy_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * psy_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (average)
rows.formula: (us_dalys_unadjusted * us_evidence_adj + cam_dalys_unadjusted * cam_evidence_adj + psy_dalys_unadjusted * psy_evidence_adj + oth_dalys_unadjusted * oth_evidence_adj) / (us_dalys_unadjusted + cam_dalys_unadjusted + psy_dalys_unadjusted + oth_dalys_unadjusted)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row.

rows.label: Counterfactual adjustment (average)
rows.formula: (us_dalys_unadjusted * us_counterfactual_adj + cam_dalys_unadjusted * cam_counterfactual_adj + psy_dalys_unadjusted * psy_counterfactual_adj + oth_dalys_unadjusted * oth_counterfactual_adj) / (us_dalys_unadjusted + cam_dalys_unadjusted + psy_dalys_unadjusted + oth_dalys_unadjusted)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row.

rows.label: KIND's share of the resources (average)
rows.formula: (us_dalys_unadjusted * us_attribution_share + cam_dalys_unadjusted * cam_attribution_share + psy_dalys_unadjusted * psy_attribution_share + oth_dalys_unadjusted * oth_attribution_share) / (us_dalys_unadjusted + cam_dalys_unadjusted + psy_dalys_unadjusted + oth_dalys_unadjusted)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row.

rows.label: Attribution share
rows.explainer: KIND's share of the resources behind the outcome: the outcome-weighted average of the branches' shares, for reading only.

rows.label: Missing-data step (average)
rows.formula: (us_dalys_unadjusted * us_missing_data_adj + cam_dalys_unadjusted * cam_missing_data_adj + psy_dalys_unadjusted * psy_missing_data_adj + oth_dalys_unadjusted * oth_missing_data_adj) / (us_dalys_unadjusted + cam_dalys_unadjusted + psy_dalys_unadjusted + oth_dalys_unadjusted)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row. Every branch is thin.

rows.label: Total adjustment (average)
rows.formula: (us_dalys_unadjusted * us_total_adj + cam_dalys_unadjusted * cam_total_adj + psy_dalys_unadjusted * psy_total_adj + oth_dalys_unadjusted * oth_total_adj) / (us_dalys_unadjusted + cam_dalys_unadjusted + psy_dalys_unadjusted + oth_dalys_unadjusted)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row.

rows.label: Know Your Rights orientations and legal screenings in federal custody, as a share
rows.explainer: KIND gave Know Your Rights orientations to 6,500 children in federal custody in 2024 (report, p. 5), with screenings that flag trafficking and abuse; most of those children never become KIND clients. Worth little each against a case won: 2%, from 0 to 6%.

rows.label: Wellbeing of security from removal beyond consumption, as a share
rows.explainer: Consumption misses the relief of no longer fearing removal and of a future in one place: when mothers became eligible for deferred action (DACA), their children's diagnoses of adjustment and anxiety disorders fell by more than half (Hainmueller et al., Science 2017), and eligible adults reported less psychological distress (Venkataramani et al., Lancet Public Health 2017). 15%, from 0 to 40%.

rows.label: Social services for US clients, as a share
rows.explainer: KIND linked 2,274 children to health care, schooling, food and housing and ran therapeutic groups with 4,177 attendances in 2024 (report, p. 9); what that adds beyond the legal case: 3%, from 0 to 10%.

rows.label: Remittances to the families at home, as a share
rows.explainer: A young person who stays and works in the US sends money home, where it raises a much poorer household's consumption: remittances are about a fifth of GDP in Honduras, El Salvador and Guatemala (World Bank). The model counts only the client's own consumption; 6%, from 0 to 20%, larger than the 3% for IRAP's refugees because Central American migrants remit more.

rows.label: Gender and Migration Initiative, as a share
rows.explainer: KIND's prevention programme against gender-based violence for adolescent girls in Guatemala and Honduras (a curriculum guide, peer and community educator training; report, p. 7) publishes no reach; prevention curricula of this kind show small effects on violence. A small part of the regional spending: 1%, from 0 to 3%.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: The sum of the five shares above.
